newsitem.title: USA: UNITED HEALTHCARE Q2 EARNINGS HIT HMO GROUP.
newsitem.headline: UNITED HEALTHCARE Q2 EARNINGS HIT HMO GROUP.

text.p: The HMO sector lost its footing Thursday after the market digested the second disappointing second quarter earnings report this week, this time from United HealthCare Corp

United Healthcare was off seven to 51-1/16. The Minneapolis company earlier Thursday said lagging margins in several markets curbed earnings growth in the quarter and were likely to be "a drag on earnings for the remainder of 1997."
Although the company matched Wall Street earnings expectations of $0.57 per share for the quarter, analysts said they were disappointed with the quality of those earnings.

On Tuesday, shares of Aetna Inc fell 14-1/4 to 102-3/4 after the company said higher premium rates in its Aetna U.S. Healthcare unit were more than offset in the second quarter by increases in commercial and Medicare HMO medical costs.

Aetna's shares continued to slide Thursday after the United HealthCare report, off 4-7/16 to 97-9/16 in afternoon trading. All told, Aetna's stock has slumped over 16 percent from Monday's closing price of 117.
Oxford Health Plans Inc got caught in the Aetna downdraft Tuesday despite its own release of slightly higher than expected second quarter earnings the same morning, losing 3-11/16.
Concerns that rising medical costs at Aetna and United HealthCare might indicate a sector-wide obstacle dragged Oxford down another 4-3/4 to 74-1/2 late Thursday.
"We've had two or three down days in the (HMO) group, and it all started with Aetna guiding earnings estimates lower," said Gary Frazier, a Bear, Stearns managing director.
Frazier noted that Aetna's medical loss ratio increased one percent sequentially from 82.6 percent in the 1997 first quarter to 83.6 percent in the second quarter.

And United HealthCare's medical loss ratio rose 30 basis points to 84.7 percent from the previous quarter. The ratio is a measure of the portion of premium revenues paid out to cover medical costs of members.

"United and Aetna are bellwethers, so people are concerned their problems could be affecting the industry," Frazier said, adding he would probably trim his 1997 earnings estimate for the company to about $2.25 per share from $2.40.

Joseph France, a health care analyst for CS First Boston, said he would also trim his United HealthCare estimates, noting the company expected margins to continue lagging for the rest of 1997 in its Maryland, Rhode Island and Gulf Coast markets.
In addition, France said the company's effective earnings were exaggerated 1.5 cents per share by a reduction in its tax rate from 39 percent in the first quarter to 37 percent in the second quarter.
